note: Authored fallback insight-card sets for all nine scenes, keyed by scene id then cross-reference. Reviewed and approved by Keith, 2026-07-29. These are NOT the shipped scoring key for a live encounter; at runtime Gloo generates a set per encounter, grounded in the curated note. Curated notes are not duplicated here, they live in daniel-1.refs.json keyed by the same scene id and ref.

constraints.note: Same constraints the runtime schema validator enforces on generated output. A card scoring 0 must contradict the passage or import a claim absent from it. A statement that is true of the passage but merely absent from the curated note is never a valid distractor: it would score 0 and punish a player for reading well.

cards.text: Kings frames the invasion as God's judgment on Judah, not just Babylon's ambition.
The same invasion is told twice in Scripture, so Daniel 1:1 sits inside a longer history.
Judah's sin had been building for generations before this moment.
Babylon attacked out of nowhere, and Judah had done nothing that led to it.
Kings says Jehoiakim defeated Nebuchadnezzar and drove him out of Judah.
The invasion happened because God had abandoned his promises to Israel for good.
Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God's servant, so the empire is a tool in God's hand, not his rival.
Judah had been warned for more than twenty years before Babylon ever arrived.
The exile is given a limit: seventy years.
Jeremiah promised Judah that Babylon would never reach Jerusalem.
The exile was announced as permanent, with no end in sight.
Jeremiah gave his warning only days before the invasion, leaving no time to turn back.
The psalm shows "the Lord gave" in Daniel 1:2 is a pattern, not a one-off: God has handed his people to their enemies before, whenever they kept turning away.
What looks like Babylon's victory in Daniel 1:2 is, in the psalm's words, God's own anger at work; the conqueror isn't the real actor.
The psalm's phrase, God "handed them over" to the nations, is the same move Daniel 1:2 describes: the treasures given into Babylon's hand.
The psalm's long cycle of rebellion and defeat is the backstory that makes sense of the Temple treasures leaving Jerusalem.
The psalm proves Daniel 1:2 wrong: God's people had never been conquered before Babylon came.
The psalm says God handed his people over even though they had stayed faithful to him.
Isaiah asks the exact question Daniel 1:2 raises (who let the plunderers in?) and answers it: the LORD did, because his people wouldn't follow him.
Read with Isaiah, "the Lord gave" is discipline with a purpose, not evidence that Babylon's god won the day.
Isaiah grieves that the people went through the fire and didn't take it to heart: the question now facing every exile watching the vessels leave.
Isaiah says the LORD wanted to stop the plundering but was unable to.
Isaiah blames the plunder entirely on Babylon's greed, with God nowhere in the story.
Isaiah promises the temple treasures would be returned within a year.
The royal youths taken in Daniel 1:3 are exactly who Isaiah told Hezekiah would one day serve in Babylon's palace; this scene is that old warning landing.
Because Isaiah saw it coming generations ahead, Daniel's selection isn't random cruelty; God was never out of the loop.
Hezekiah proudly showing off his treasures is the small moment of pride at the root of this scene's consequences.
The warning said "your sons," and the delay is part of the story: it lands generations later, on Daniel's generation.
Isaiah's warning was about Egypt, so Babylon's palace program has nothing to do with it.
Isaiah promised Hezekiah that no descendant of Judah's kings would ever serve in Babylon.
Moses shows what Daniel's training could become: a Hebrew taught all the empire's wisdom who still belonged completely to God.
If God turned Egypt's education into Moses' preparation, then Babylon's curriculum in Daniel 1:4 isn't automatically the enemy.
Like the youths in Daniel 1:4, Moses was picked young and shaped by a foreign court for years before God's purpose came into view.
Moses' story proves that learning a pagan culture's wisdom always ends in losing your faith.
Stephen says Moses refused Egypt's schooling, so Daniel should refuse Babylon's.
Stephen credits Egypt's education, not God, with rescuing Israel.
Jehoiachin's lifelong ration from Babylon's table shows what the arrangement in Daniel 1:5 makes of a person: a dependent of the empire, for good.
Judah's own king accepted the very provision Daniel is about to refuse; the comparison shows how unusual Daniel's coming choice really is.
Kings ends its whole story with an exile at the empire's table, leaving open the question Daniel 1 picks up: can you live on Babylon's food and still belong to God?
Jehoiachin's seat "above the other kings" shows Babylon used its table to rank people; the same table is now being set for Daniel.
Kings says Jehoiachin refused the ration and starved rather than eat Babylon's food.
Kings condemns Jehoiachin's ration as the sin that defiled him beyond recovery.
Ezekiel shows who this unknown young man in Daniel 1:6 will become: a fellow exile was already naming Daniel beside Noah and Job as the measure of righteousness.
The introduction in Daniel 1:6 is quiet, but Ezekiel proves Daniel's faithfulness was famous among the captives in his own lifetime.
Ezekiel's sober point (even the most righteous rescue only themselves) frames what four faithful men can and can't do for a judged nation.
Ezekiel lists Daniel as a warning about the cost of compromising in exile.
Ezekiel had never heard of Daniel, which shows the four were unknown among the exiles.
Ezekiel promises that Daniel's righteousness would spare Jerusalem from judgment.
Joseph took an Egyptian name and everything that came with it, and stayed God's man: the hopeful answer to what Babylon is trying in Daniel 1:7.
Pharaoh's renaming never reached Joseph's identity, which means Nebuchadnezzar's renaming doesn't have to reach Daniel's.
Joseph shows a forced foreign name can even sit alongside serving God at the empire's highest level.
Joseph's new name came bundled with real advancement, as Daniel's will, and neither gift bought the empire a soul.
Joseph's story warns that accepting a foreign name is the first step to losing your faith.
Genesis shows the renaming worked: Joseph gradually forgot the God of his fathers.
Nebuchadnezzar renamed Judah's own king to show he owned him, which reveals what the new names in Daniel 1:7 are really claiming.
Same king, same move: the renaming of Daniel's friends is imperial branding, not Babylonian hospitality.
Kings records the renaming right beside the deportations; new names were part of the same conquest.
Kings shows renaming was an honor Babylon reserved for its most trusted friends.
Kings says Babylon left Judah's kings and nobles their own names.
The renamed Zedekiah ruled with full independence, proving the new names carried no claim.
"God caused the official to show favor" in Daniel 1:9 is Joseph's story replaying: God gave Joseph the same favor with his prison warden.
Both stories put God behind the official's kindness: the sympathy Daniel meets isn't luck or charm, it's a pattern.
Joseph's favor came inside a prison and Daniel's inside a captivity; God's help meets his people in hard places, not just out of them.
In both stories the favor arrives when the believer is at his most powerless: a prisoner, and a captive teenager.
Joseph earned the warden's trust entirely on his own, showing Daniel's favor needed no help from God.
Genesis says the warden mistreated Joseph until Pharaoh finally intervened.
The proverb names the official's exact bind in Daniel 1:10: "I'm afraid of the king" is the fear-of-people trap closing in real time.
Daniel is the proverb's other half in action: trusting the LORD is what makes his quiet courage possible.
The proverb turns the scene into a study in contrast: two men under the same king, one trapped and one safe.
The proverb sides with the official; fearing the king is the wisest course.
The proverb says trusting God means never having to deal with dangerous people.
The proverb promises the official that the king could never actually harm him.
Daniel's ten days of vegetables runs on the wilderness lesson: real life comes from depending on God, not from a full plate.
God once used hunger and manna to teach his people trust, which reframes the plain menu in Daniel 1:12 as training, not deprivation.
The manna years were a test "to know what was in your heart," which is exactly what ten days of vegetables will reveal about the four.
Israel thrived for years on nothing but God's provision, a preview of four exiles thriving on vegetables and water.
Deuteronomy teaches that eating plain food is what makes a person righteous.
The wilderness story shows God expects his people to demand rich food as their right.
Hebrews names the trade Daniel is making at the table: Moses gave up palace pleasures because faithfulness is worth more than an empire's treasures.
Moses could make the trade because he was looking ahead to God's reward, the same long view that makes ten days of vegetables an easy call.
Both men had full access to the empire's best and turned it down from the inside; this isn't envy talking, it's choice.
Hebrews says Moses kept his palace privileges, proving God's people should accept an empire's comforts.
Hebrews presents Moses' choice as a loss he regretted for the rest of his life.
The letter says Moses left Egypt's pleasures because he had grown bored of them.
Jesus' answer in the desert names what Daniel's menu test is really about: life comes from every word from God's mouth, not just from food.
Both refusals happen with the food within arm's reach; faithfulness shows itself right at the point of appetite.
Jesus carries through a forty-day fast the same faithfulness Daniel practices at a dinner table: the pattern, completed.
Jesus was led into his hunger by the Spirit: a test inside God's plan, like Daniel's, not outside it.
Matthew says Jesus gave in and made the bread, showing appetite always wins in the end.
Jesus' example teaches that God's servants are above needing to eat.
James states the rule behind Daniel 1:17: wisdom is God's gift to anyone who asks, which is why the verse credits God and not the curriculum.
"God gives generously to all without finding fault" explains how four exiles could excel inside a system stacked against them.
James shows the gift in Daniel 1:17 wasn't a one-time exception; the same offer stands open to anyone who asks.
James says wisdom must be earned through study alone, correcting Daniel 1:17's claim that God gave it.
James warns that God resents being asked for wisdom too often.
James limits God's gift of wisdom to priests and trained scholars.
The proverb is Daniel 1:17 in one line: the LORD gives wisdom, so the four's brilliance traces to God, not to Babylon's training.
"Knowledge and understanding from his mouth" is exactly how Daniel 1:17 describes what the four received: given, not achieved.
The proverb quietly demotes Babylon's curriculum from source to setting: the place wisdom showed up, not where it came from.
The proverb credits wisdom to the wise themselves, exactly as Babylon credits its experts.
Proverbs says God keeps wisdom to himself and shares none of it.
The proverb teaches that pagan schooling blocks God's gift of wisdom.
Joseph shows what Daniel's gift for dreams is and where it comes from: "it's not in me; God will give the answer."
Two Hebrews in foreign courts who understand dreams, both pointing the credit the same direction; Joseph confirms Daniel 1:17's "God gave."
Joseph's gift opened doors to power in Egypt, a preview of where Daniel's understanding of visions will take him in Babylon.
It was a king's impossible question that showcased Joseph's gift, and the king's questions will do the same for Daniel's.
Joseph claimed the interpreting skill as his own talent, the opposite of what Daniel 1:17 says.
Genesis says Joseph learned dream interpretation in Egypt's dream-schools.
The proverb reads Daniel 1:19 like a caption: the truly skilled end up serving before kings, and that's exactly where the four now stand.
Three years of diligence plus God's gift is how the proverb's promise came true for four captives with no connections.
The proverb makes their placement a matter of wisdom's order, not Babylon's favor; skill is what put them in that room.
The proverb says only noble birth puts a person before kings, so the four must have had royal patrons.
The proverb warns the skilled to stay far away from kings.
The proverb promises that the diligent will be spared from ever serving foreign rulers.
Hannah's song names what Daniel 1:19 shows: God lifts the lowly from the dust to seat them among princes, and here captives stand in the throne room.
The song reveals whose hand is behind the promotion: not Babylon's exam, but the God who raises up and brings low.
The song's other half hangs over the scene too: the proud and mighty, Babylon included, don't stay on top forever.
Hannah sang it over one answered prayer, and it kept coming true at the scale of nations; the throne room shows the song still working.
Hannah's song teaches that the strong earn their place, so the four rose on merit alone with God uninvolved.
The song says God leaves thrones and empires to run themselves.
Jesus' promise (wisdom no opponent can withstand, before kings) is the same gift on display when no one in Babylon measures up to the four.
The promise reframes Daniel's exam: standing before a king isn't just a test, it's a place God equips his people to represent him.
Jesus frames it around testifying under threat, which sharpens what Daniel's calm before Nebuchadnezzar is previewing.
Jesus promises his followers they will never have to stand before kings the way Daniel did.
Jesus says such wisdom must be carefully prepared and memorized in advance.
Jesus limits the promise to friendly audiences, not hostile rulers.
Isaiah's taunt explains the "ten times better" of Daniel 1:20: Babylon's celebrated astrologers can't save the city or even themselves.
The king is measuring the four against experts God has already declared hollow; the contest was decided before it began.
Isaiah pictures them worn out by a lifetime of consultations that rescue no one: the very colleagues Daniel now out-performs.
Isaiah expects Babylon's astrologers to read the stars correctly and save the city.
Isaiah rates the astrologers' wisdom as equal to the wisdom God gives.
Isaiah praises Babylon for its diligent study of the stars.
The psalm gives away the secret behind "ten times better": God's word makes a person wiser than enemies, teachers, and even the ancients.
The psalm relocates the four's edge: not raw talent, not the king's curriculum, but a life shaped by God's word.
"Wiser than my own teachers" is precisely what the king's testing exposed in Babylon's classrooms.
The psalmist's edge is a daily practice of staying in God's word; the four's advantage is a habit, not a one-time gift.
The psalmist admits his teachers and the ancients were wiser than he could ever become.
The psalm credits the psalmist's wisdom to studying his enemies' tactics.
Mordecai shows what Daniel 1:21's quiet last line means: a faithful Jew can not only survive an empire but endure at the very top of it.
Both men's standing was for their people, not themselves; endurance at court, in Scripture, is a post of service.
Both stories got stamped into the empire's own records; the world's chronicles end up testifying about God's people.
Esther shows Mordecai's rise required abandoning his people and their identity.
Esther ends with Mordecai cast out of the court, a warning to exiles who serve kings.
The record says Mordecai used his position to enrich himself at his people's expense.
